messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh is a 32-year-old South Asian man who has been working as a housekeeper for several years. He is married and his life was relatively stable until he experienced a traumatic event—a mugging—that has profoundly altered how he perceives the world around him. One chilly evening, Rajesh was walking home from work when he was suddenly confronted by two men demanding his wallet. In the struggle that ensued, one of the assailants hit him on the head with a blunt object, causing severe pain and injury. The memory of this event is exceptionally vivid; every detail comes back to him in sharp relief, including the cold metal of the object hitting his skull and the fear he felt as he realized his life was in danger. Since that night, Rajesh has found it almost impossible to talk about what happened without feeling overwhelmed by physical pain. The memory resurfaces often, triggered by anything reminiscent of the event—dark alleys on his way home from work or a sudden loud noise in an otherwise quiet room. When these memories return, he feels the same intense physical discomfort as if the trauma were happening all over again. Rajesh’s traumatic experience has also deeply affected his trust in others. He now believes that people are not what they seem and can’t be trusted. This mistrust is pervasive; it colors every interaction he has, making him wary of even the most benign encounters. As a housekeeper, Rajesh frequently finds himself in situations where he must engage with new clients or interact with strangers in public spaces. Each encounter feels like walking on eggshells because he’s certain that danger lurks behind every smile. The vividness and painful recollections of the mugging have only reinforced his negative appraisals. Every time a memory resurfaces, Rajesh is reminded of how unsafe the world can be, solidifying his belief that people are inherently untrustworthy. This cycle has left him feeling isolated and on edge, constantly scanning for signs of potential threats. Rajesh’s sense of distrust and danger exacerbates his memory disturbances. When he experiences vivid flashbacks or intrusive thoughts, it fuels his negative beliefs about the world, making him even more guarded and suspicious. He often wakes up in a cold sweat, replaying the event over and over again, each time reinforcing his belief that the world is dangerous. These ongoing fears have begun to affect his work. Rajesh has started skipping certain shifts or avoiding parts of his job that require walking alone at night, leading to conflicts with his employers. His marriage has also been strained; he keeps to himself more often and avoids social situations, which has left his wife feeling concerned about his wellbeing. Despite these challenges, Rajesh’s deteriorating mental state finally prompted him to seek help. He is most afraid of never being able to feel safe again and living with constant vigilance. At the same time, he hopes that therapy might provide a way to manage his memories and regain some trust in others and in life itself. In summary, Rajesh’s experience has left him with vivid, painful memories of the mugging, which fuel his deeply ingrained beliefs about the world being dangerous and untrustworthy. This cycle of negative appraisals and intrusive memories has significantly impacted his daily functioning and relationships, leading to a decision to seek psychological help in order to regain some semblance of normalcy and safety in his life.
